subject: Questions about staggered TTL rollback and cross-border backup/restore implications
messages:
From: Sarah Willis <sarah.willis@finbank.com>
To: tessa_morgan <tessa_morgan@redwood.ai>
Cc: FinBank Compliance Team <compliance@finbank.com>
Date: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 08:05:12 +0000
Subject: Clarify: staggered TTL rollback and cross-border backup/restore implications

Hi Tessa,

Thanks for taking this — we’re working through an audit question that popped up after a recent data-retention review. Two quick items the auditors asked us to confirm for EU-resident backups:  

1) If a TTL is changed (eg. customer requests retention shortened) and we do a staggered rollback across regions, what is the end-to-end timeline from the moment the TTL is updated to the point where data is fully expunged from all replicas? We need the upper bound for our risk assessment.

2) During the propagation window there is concern about restore consistency: if we attempt to restore a snapshot taken before the TTL change but the expunge has started in region A and not yet in region B, will the restore be guaranteed to return the pre-change data? What are the failure modes?

The auditors also requested: sample audit evidence (expunge logs, manifest entries, and any tamper-evident proof we can provide). Can you outline what Redwood can provide and an expected delivery time?

Ideally we’d like a short summary and then a technical statement we can attach to the audit.

Appreciate it — we’ve got a deadline next Friday so anything you can do to speed this is helpful.

—Sarah
Sarah Willis
Lead, Compliance Risk
FinBank

From: tessa_morgan <tessa_morgan@redwood.ai>
To: Sarah Willis <sarah.willis@finbank.com>
Cc: karthik_iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 10:22:07 +0000
Subject: Re: Clarify: staggered TTL rollback and cross-border backup/restore implications

Hi Sarah — thanks for the clear asks. Short answer up front: we can provide an audit-ready statement and supporting artifacts; the worst-case expunge window is longer than the metadata tombstone window and depends on replication and retention waves. I’m looping in Karthik for the precise timeline and evidence locations.

High-level summary for your auditors (can be used as a technical statement):
- TTL update & tombstone creation: immediate once the retention change is applied to the account metadata.
- Replica marking: replicas are marked for expiration quickly (usually within minutes), but physical expunge is performed by asynchronous regional background waves.
- Typical expunge completion: per-region background waves run on a schedule; conservative upper bound is 7 days for full expunge across all replicas in cross-region configurations (EU <-> US) depending on backlog and retention locks.
- Restore guarantees: snapshots taken before the TTL change remain restorable while any replica containing the snapshot has not been fully expunged. If any replica is expunged before the restore attempts to reconstruct from remaining replicas, a full restore may fail or produce an incomplete dataset. Legal holds and preservation flags prevent expunge.

Requested evidence we can provide: expunge operation logs, per-replica manifest entries, tombstone creation timestamps, and audit traces showing retention-change API calls. Karthik — can you add specific path names and sample IDs we should give FinBank?

Action items:  
- Karthik to provide detailed timeline matrix + sample log ids (we’ll attach a table).
- I’ll produce a two-paragraph technical statement and a short playbook for your auditors.

Attaching an evidence checklist template to speed collection (see later emails).

Best,
Tessa Morgan
Director, Customer Reliability
Redwood Inference

From: karthik_iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>
To: tessa_morgan <tessa_morgan@redwood.ai>, Sarah Willis <sarah.willis@finbank.com>
Date: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 14:43:01 +0000
Subject: Re: Clarify: staggered TTL rollback and cross-border backup/restore implications

Sarah / Tessa — technical details and evidence pointers below. Quoting the original request for context.

Summary timeline (typical, conservative upper bounds):
- 0s: TTL change applied to account metadata — tombstone marker created on master control-plane immediately.
- 0–5 min: Control plane issues change events to region controllers; replicas receive \"marked-for-expunge\" flag.
- 1–6 hr: Cross-region replication of the marker completed in most cases (network dependent).
- 24–72 hr: Per-region background sweeper picks up marked objects and queues them for physical expunge; this depends on queue backlog and maintenance windows.
- 3–7 days: Full physical expunge of all replicas in low-priority/low-throughput regions or during heavy maintenance/backlog. We use 7 days as a conservative SLA upper bound for multi-region configurations.

Restore behaviour and risk modes:  
- If a restore job starts while at least one replica still has intact objects, the system will perform a cross-replica rebuild and return the snapshot contents. In practice this is successful when the expunge wave has not yet permanently deleted the last replica.
- If the expunge wave has completed in all replicas for a snapshot, the data is unrecoverable via normal restore (only extraordinary forensics or customer-archived copies would help).
- Edge case: staggered TTL rollback where region A expunges earlier than region B can lead to partial restores if cross-replica repair is interrupted. We mitigate with transfer-locks during restore attempts but cannot guarantee atomicity across clouds if full expunge has occurred.

Legal hold & preservation: setting a preservation/hold flag on an account or object immediately stops background expunge for that object. The hold is respected across control-plane and replicated to region controllers. Hold removal must be explicit and is auditable.

Evidence artifacts we can provide (samples included in attachment):
- expunge-timeline-table.xlsx: per-operation timestamps, replica IDs, region codes. (sample rows attached)
- Audit log path: s3://redwood-audit/expunge-ops/<account-id>/2026/11/19/expunge-log-<op-id>.json
- Manifest entries path: s3://redwood-manifests/<account-id>/snapshots/<snapshot-id>.manifest
- Tombstone markers & tombstone API call IDs (control-plane event ids) — we’ll provide a short mapping table.

Estimated delivery to you: 48 hours for a packaged zip with the table + three sample logs + the technical statement. If you need certified/attested copies for an external audit, allow additional time for notarization.

Let me know the FinBank account-id and any preferred sample snapshot ids and I’ll stage the artifacts.

—Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Senior SRE, Redwood Inference

Sarah — quick summary and next steps for your audit packet.

Executive summary (one paragraph for auditors):
Redwood applies TTL changes immediately at the control plane which creates tombstone markers. Physical deletion of backup data is performed asynchronously by region-specific background expunge processes; for multi-region configurations Redwood uses conservative operational windows and provides evidence of per-region expunge events. While a snapshot remains present on at least one replica it is restorable; once a snapshot is fully expunged from all replicas it is irrecoverable. Legal preservation flags prevent expunge and are replicated across regions.

Deliverables we’ll provide (target: within 48 hours):
- Packaged evidence zip: expunge-timeline-table.xlsx, three sample expunge logs (region-level), and two manifest entries.
- Technical statement (2 paragraphs) for your audit pack.
- Short playbook (redwood-backup-playbook.pdf) describing recommended steps if auditors want to perform a restore test during propagation windows.

Requested info from FinBank: account-id (for artifact extraction) and two snapshot-ids you want sampled. If you prefer we’ll include the most recent snapshot prior to your retention-change event.

I’m attaching the technical evidence checklist and the expunge-timeline spreadsheet for your review; once you confirm account-id and snapshot ids I’ll trigger the artifact extraction. Also created JIRA-OPS-1942 to track this request internally.
